reason: The provided sources contain multiple matching facts across independent sites supporting the story of William Herschel's discovery of Uranus and his attempt to name it after King George III.
story: In March 1781, German-born musician and amateur astronomer William Herschel was scanning the night sky from his home garden in Bath, England, using a homemade reflecting telescope. He spotted a faint, disk-like object moving slowly against the background stars. At first, Herschel assumed he had discovered a new comet. However, orbit calculations by fellow astronomers soon proved the object moved in a nearly circular path around the Sun, revealing it as the first planet discovered since antiquity. By uncovering a world orbiting twice as far out as Saturn, Herschel instantly doubled the known size of the Solar System. Eager to honor his royal patron, Herschel proposed naming the seventh planet 'Georgium Sidus' (George's Star) after King George III. While King George rewarded him with an annual stipend, international astronomers strongly rejected naming a planet after a British monarch. Ultimately, German astronomer Johann Elert Bode's suggestion took hold, officially naming the ice giant Uranus.
angle: Discoverer William Herschel originally named the planet Uranus 'George's Star' after King George III, but international astronomers refused to name a planet after the British monarch.

claims.claim: William Herschel was born in Hanover and moved to England in 1757 to work as a musician.
Herschel constructed his own reflecting telescopes to survey the night sky.
On March 13, 1781, Herschel observed a new faint object that moved slowly relative to background stars.
Herschel made his discovery observation from the garden of his home in Bath, England.
Herschel initially reported and believed the newly discovered object was a comet.
Calculations of the object's orbit showed it was nearly circular around the Sun, proving it was a planet.
Uranus was the first planet discovered using a telescope and the first found since antiquity.
The discovery of Uranus doubled the known size of the Solar System.
Herschel proposed naming the new planet Georgium Sidus (George's Star) in honor of King George III.
Herschel's proposed royal name was rejected outside Britain by astronomers in other countries.
German astronomer Johann Elert Bode proposed the name Uranus, following classical mythological naming conventions.
King George III awarded Herschel an annual stipend and membership in the Royal Society following the discovery.
Uranus takes approximately 84 Earth years to complete one orbit around the Sun.
Astronomer Royal Nevil Maskelyne confessed he was unsure whether to call the object a planet or a comet after Herschel notified him.
